segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How would you say, I want to carry on? Now you think, carry on, I don't know this.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, one of the skills we want to really make use of these convertible words is to find the Latin equivalent of carry on.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: I want to carry on, I want to go on, I want to... What is the Latin word that we could use here?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Nothing comes to mind?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Blank.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So think of...

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Ah, continue.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Ah. So you could think of a -tion word that has something to do with carrying on, and make...

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Continuation.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Exactly. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, I want to continue?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Quiero continuar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Quiero continuar. I want to continue it?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Quiero continuarlo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. I'm trying to continue.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: I've already forgotten what trying is.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, it's not about remembering, it's about knowing how to find it. So, there are a few things you could think about that when we discussed this word that could lead you back to it. And the important thing is to take that time to have those thoughts rather than just, 'Oh, do I know it? Do I not?'

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Intención.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Intención. There wasn't a rule here because it doesn't finish -ation, our rule was for ones that finish -ation, but it was very similar. Do you remember what it is now? I try?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So it ends in -o, like...

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Ah, intento.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Intento. Good, so that's I try. We want to see first if we can find it relaxed, not, you know, if your brain locks on 'Do I remember it or don't I?', game over. But if you go, 'Okay, what was that related to? What was that about?' and to see what pops up, then you're much more likely to get it. So intento, intento is I try.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: I try or I'm trying to continue?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Intento continuar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Intento continuar. What is demostración? Demostración?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Demonstration.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Demonstration. Do you notice something different though? The some change here, demostración?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: There's no n.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good, there's no n. Demostración. So how would you say to demonstrate?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Demostrar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Demostrar. Now, if you get rid of that de-, how would it sound?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Mostrar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Mostrar, and that means to show. To show, mostrar. So we might think again, mostrar has no connection that we can hook onto.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: But usually when we have a look, we can find some connection through English, Latin English, that helps us interiorize mostrar, to show.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: The word for something is algo, algo. A-L-G-O, algo.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Algo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Algo, good. What was the word for you like in I love you? How was I love you?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Te quiero.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Te quiero, so it was te. So how would you say, I want to show you something? In this order: I want to show you something.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Quiero mostrarte algo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Quiero mostrarte algo. I want to show you something. What again was I go, I'm going, and it was related to voyage, we said?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Voy?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: The beginning bit of voyage. And you're mostly going to hear it pronounced more like a soft B, voy, voy.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Voy.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now, just as in English we say I'm going to when we talk about the future—I'm going to continue, I'm going to eat later—we can do exactly the same thing in Spanish.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: The only difference is that even though for example if we use continue, continuar, continuar means to continue, in Spanish we say voy a continuar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: It's actually because voy is a verb of movement. When we are putting a to-form, a verb that is to something like continuar, after a verb of movement, a verb that have some kind of motion in its in its meaning like voy, I'm going, Spanish wants to show this feeling of motion. So you say I'm going to, and you put the to for that movement, even if you're not actually moving and you're just using it to speak about the future.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, if you want to say, for example, I'm going to confiscate it. I'm going to confiscate it?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Voy a confiscarlo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Voy a confiscarlo. Very good. How would you say, I'm going to examine it? I'm going to examine it?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Voy a examinarlo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Voy a examinarlo. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now, we said lo is it or him. Now the plural of him is them. This is not very obvious in English because him and them, they look very different as words. We don't ever think of them as the plural of him or of her, but it is. It's very obvious in Spanish.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Lo means him or it, and if you want to get them, if you want to make it plural, what do you think you might do?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Just add the s? Los.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Los. Good. So now we have the word for them. To see is ver, ver. We have view in English, like view, ver. So how would you say, I want to see them?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Quiero a verlos?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Mm, why a here?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Quiero verlos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Quiero verlos. So ver is to see. If you say, I'm going to see them, how is it going to be?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Voy a verlos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Voy a verlos. But if you say, I want to see them?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Quiero verlos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And if you say, I'm trying to see them?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Intento verlos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. No a. Intento verlos, because ver is to see. To try, so try in its to-form, to try, is intentar, intentar. This is to try.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So how would you say, I want to try?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Quiero intentar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. I'm going to try?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Voy a intentar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good, with a, voy a intentar. I'm going to try to see them? I'm going to try to see them?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Voy a intentar a verlos. No, verlos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Very good.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Voy intentar... Voy a intentar verlos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Voy a intentar verlos. Good. Let me give you another example of a verb that connects with this a, so voy isn't isolated. We can understand the concept better if we see another verb of movement. So another verb of movement is pasar. What do you think pasar means?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Is it to pass?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Ah. Yes.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Pasar is to pass and to pass by. So, I'm going to pass by to visit you. I'm going to pass by to visit you. How would we say this? So the first bit is, I'm going?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Voy.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. I'm going to pass by?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: A pasar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. To visit you?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Visitarlo. Visitarte.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Te. Well actually, lo other than him and it can also mean formal you. So if you're speaking formally, you can use this lo as well.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: But I want to go back to pasar. Pasar is a verb of movement. Let's let's take the sentence again from the beginning. The whole sentence is, I am going to pass by to visit you.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Voy a... so it's voy a pasar a visitarlo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Lo if you are speaking formally, or te if you are speaking informally. Voy a pasar a visitarte. Voy a pasar a visitarlo, which would mean him, it, or you formal.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How would you say formal, by the way, in Spanish?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Formal.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And formally?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Formalmente.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Very good. Now, if you want to say, I am going to try to pass by to visit you, we have to think which ones we're going to use this a with and which one's not, which is a great exercise for us to internalize this rule. So, I am going to try?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Voy a intentar...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: To pass by?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: A... no. Voy a intentar pasar...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: To visit you?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: A visitarte.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Very good. So we learned our rule.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Voy a intentar pasar a visitarte. It's not many times that we have something between the verbs, so there's not going to be a lot of rules like this, don't worry. But this one's important because there are many important verbs of motion that we will be putting this a after.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How how was to demonstrate again?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Demostrar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And what happened to that n?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Ah, demostrar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Demostrar. And what is to show? You get rid of the...

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Mostrar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Mostrar. And the word for something, I mentioned was algo, algo.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Algo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Something. I want to show you something. Let's speak informally. I want to show you something, so we're going to use te.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Quiero mostrarte algo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. I want to show you something. Quiero mostrarte algo. So maybe you call somebody and you say like, 'Where are you? I'm at home.' 'Okay, I want to pass by to show you something. I want to pass by to show you something.'

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Quiero pasar a... What was it? I want to...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: To to show you something.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Mostrarte algo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Quiero pasar a—because we have a verb of movement—mostrarte algo. So if we're connecting a verb of movement to another verb, we connect using this this extra a, to. Quiero pasar a mostrarte algo. Good.
